title: Krispy Kreme 1Q Adjusted EBITDA Jumps 38% Amid Turnaround
content:
By Daniella Parra

Krispy Kreme, Inc. (Nasdaq: DNUT) said adjusted EBITDA rose 38 percent in the first quarter to $33.1 million from a year earlier amid a company turnaround.

Net revenue fell 2.2 percent to $367 million, it said, adding that the company is seeing wider adoption of its capital-light international franchise model.

“The first quarter highlighted significant progress across every pillar of our turnaround plan,” said Krispy Kreme CEO Josh Charlesworth. “We reduced net leverage, increased adjusted EBITDA margin by 260 basis points, and delivered positive free cash flow.”

title: Burger King president says fast food is 'a zero-sum game' — and BK is winning
content:
Fast food burger competition is heating up, and Burger King has notched the first big W.

Restaurant Brands (QSR) said this week its Burger King US chain delivered a 5.8% same-store sales increase in the first quarter. The result outperformed the quick-service restaurant industry by more than five points, Bernstein analyst Danilo Gargiulo said.

It also bested arch nemesis McDonald’s (MCD) — its US business posted a same-store sales increase of 3.9% in the first quarter today.

“It’s a zero-sum game. It’s not a growing category,” Burger King US and Canada president Tom Curtis said on Yahoo Finance’s Opening Bid (video above). “But we’ve proven to ourselves that if you do offer a better experience and a better core product, you can absolutely grow.”

The latest burger contest backstory: A new fast food burger battle erupted on social media in early March, and McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski led the way, going viral in a promotional video where he tried the company’s new Big Arch burger. The clip was widely mocked for his seemingly hesitant approach to eating the burger, taking an unusually small, delicate bite and repeatedly referring to the burger as a “product.”

Capitalizing on the backlash, Burger King’s Curtis released a TikTok video three days later. It featured him taking an enthusiastic bite of a Whopper and joking that the only thing missing was a “napkin.” He gave out his phone number so people could share what they thought about the brand.

He ended up talking to 1,500 people after the number share and getting tens of thousands more messages.

Curtis’s viral moment also shed light on the revamped Whopper, which has long been the company’s answer to McDonald’s Big Mac.

Burger King made several subtle but meaningful changes to its Whopper for the first time in nearly a decade. The updated burger now features a more premium, better-tasting bun and a reformulated, creamier mayonnaise. Toppings like lettuce, tomatoes, onions, and pickles are prepared to taste fresher and stack more neatly.Burger King elevated its Whopper burger. (Credit: Handout from Burger King)·Hand-out

Another major change is the packaging: Instead of being wrapped in paper, the burger is now served in a box to prevent it from getting squished and to maintain its presentation.

“When we opened up the phone lines for the guests to tell us what they wanted, they said, ‘Hey, your Whopper is great, but it’s smushed sometimes, and maybe the mayonnaise could be creamier,’” Curtis said. “We took that feedback … but [the changes] had to be nuanced. It couldn’t be a big change because the Whopper was already loved.”

Story Continues

The bottom line: Perhaps Kempczinski should take a Curtis-like bite of his food next time on camera — clearly it has worked for BK! Expect the US outperformance of Burger King versus McDonald’s to continue in the near term.

title: McDonald's will 'probably' continue offering free refills as self-serve soda machines disappear
content:
McDonald’s (MCD) is phasing out its self-serve soda fountains that allow customers to fill their own cups. By 2032, the iconic machines dispensing a choice of Hi-C, Fanta, Diet Coke, and Dr Pepper — or a mix of any of those — will be behind the counter instead of in the front.

Worried about still being able to get a free refill? According to one McDonald’s executive, you should still be able to go back for more.

“Free refills are always up to the kind of franchisee, but I count on the fact that most of them are probably going to continue to do that,” McDonald’s CFO Ian Borden told Yahoo Finance.

McDonald’s announced the soda machine phaseout in 2023, as the chain intended to create a more consistent experience for customers and crew members across delivery, app orders, kiosks, drive-through, and in restaurants. But conversation around the shift resurfaced this week as consumers began to take notice.A person holds a McDonald's Coca-Cola in a large cup. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)·Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images

“One of the things that we’ve seen over the last several years is just the growth of digital, the growth of delivery,” CEO Chris Kempczinski said on a call with investors. “That means that the kind of customer flows or customer journey and our restaurant looks a little bit different. … We are certainly working with franchisees to think about what that restaurant of the future needs to look like.”

Reassuring customers who have been vocal about the change, Borden said, “All of our consumers can be assured that when they come into McDonald’s, they’re going to get what they’re looking for.”

Meanwhile, other fast food giants have weighed in more emphatically on the matter. Restaurant Brands’ (QSR) Burger King said it plans to keep its self-service soda machines.

“When they want a refill, they can have a refill — that’s the way we feel about it,” Burger King US and Canada president Tom Curtis told Yahoo Finance. “Our consumers are telling us that they want to come into a restaurant, if they don’t have a freestyle machine they want to mix their own, we’re going to allow them to do that with the beverage dispensers that we have.”

McDonald’s phaseout is part of a new beverage strategy the company launched in late April with the debut of six specialty drinks, including refreshers and “dirty sodas,” or customizable sodas mixed with creamer and flavored syrups.

“The three refreshers and the three crafted sodas are kind of the first step in that direction,” Borden said.

title: Burger King's listening tour is paying off
content:
The burger wars are heating up. Burger King (QSR) is taking a slightly different approach, focusing on consumer input and evaluating the brand staples rather than launching new products.

Tom Curtis, Burger King President US & Canada, joins Yahoo Finance Executive Editor Brian Sozzi to discuss what’s new with the Whopper, the operational improvements driving the brand’s turnaround, and why he believes Burger King is outperforming rivals—including McDonald’s (MCD), which is signaling a potential slowdown next quarter.

Video Transcript

00:00 Speaker A

But I want to deconstruct uh a little bit this uh this burger war this morning because McDonald's is out 3. what 8% same source sales increase. You guys had a a much larger increase like but why did why did that happen?

00:12 Speaker B

Uh I don't think it's, you know, a lot of the news is around the Whopper, but I really think it's why and how it happened. Uh the listening campaign that we've been on and absolutely connecting with our guests genuinely. I think that's what's made the difference here. Not just the fact that we've elevated the Whopper.

00:34 Speaker A

What did what did you take me back to when you realized, guys, like we need to revamp this iconic sandwich. We don't necessarily need to pull a McDonald's and create something called a Big Arch that nobody's going to want to eat anyway. We have this thing on our menu that people love and it needs to be revamped. Like when when was that moment?

00:54 Speaker B

Uh well, once again, it came from the guest. So when we opened up the phone lines if you will for the for the guests to tell us what they wanted, they said, hey, your Whopper's great, but it need it's smushed sometimes. And you know, maybe the mayonnaise could be creamier, just gave us a lot of feedback and we took that feedback and elevated. I don't want to say I don't like saying revamped. I don't like saying re-engineered.

01:20 Speaker A

You're the product guy here. I'm just

01:21 Speaker B

Yeah, but but it had to be nuanced. It couldn't be a a big change because the Whopper was already loved.

01:29 Speaker A

So I how, basically, why is this new sandwich better than the Big Arch?

01:37 Speaker B

Well, okay, I'm a little bit biased here, but I think it's the right size portion. I think it's been America's favorite burger for many, many years and it's just uh it's it's got that beautiful glazed bun and the flame grilled burger. You don't get that elsewhere.

02:03 Speaker B

And uh whether it's uh one competitor's product if you will or another

02:09 Speaker A

You can't even say the name. You're not even going to say it. Like that's when I ask the Coca-Cola team to mention Pepsi Cola. They won't even say it. Um

02:16 Speaker B

Can't say the word.

02:17 Speaker A

So when you were creating that commercial, did you know it was going to go viral?

02:20 Speaker B

Uh, no idea whatsoever. And we did not we did not create create our social content to be juxtaposed to theirs. It just happened. And that's the way that social media is. You just don't know what's going to happen.

02:38 Speaker A

I don't remember the Whopper having a glaze. I used to grow up. I mean I grew up eating these things. I mean, it just did. How are you changing the experience in the restaurants? Because my interpretation from the earnings call, you are now investing a large sum of money to remodel a lot of restaurants.

02:54 Speaker B

Yep, we started that about three or four years ago and that's why we really only felt comfortable talking about the elevated brand and the elevated burger now. We needed to do the work on the experience in the restaurant.

03:19 Speaker A

I can't believe that's burg that's Burger King?

03:22 Speaker B

That's Burger King. Yep. So that's uh that's our sizzle image and that's the way that they all look now. Uh not the way they all look, but every new one coming out of the ground looks.

03:36 Speaker B

But to be very clear, and this is great news for us, we've got a long way to go till they all look that way until the experience is perfect in every restaurant. So we believe we have many years of growth ahead of us. This is the start. This isn't a great quarter. This is the start of a great story.

title: Why McDonald's may be a better consumer story than an investment play
content:
McDonald’s (MCD) topped Q1 estimates after four straight quarters of same-store sales growth, but CEO Chris Kempczinski warns business could slow next quarter.

Yahoo Finance’s Julie Hyman and Head of News Myles Udland break down why McDonald’s may be a stronger consumer story than an investor story.

Video Transcript

00:00 Speaker A

stock here is uh doing nothing. It had been higher last night on McDonald's coming out, another quarter of US same store sales growth, fourth straight quarter US same store sales growth. Those comps were up 3.9%.

00:10 Speaker A

Um, cooling off a little bit though on some headlines we're seeing from the conference call. Yes.

00:15 Speaker B

Yes, exactly. The CEO, Chris Kemp Kempczinski, yes, saying um that he expects things to be down this quarter. So that's why we are seeing like the things just slowed down from that um higher comp growth. I mean, the comp growth it sort of bottomed and then it to your point has been rising for several quarters here.

00:41 Speaker B

Um, you know, and they've been doing things like introducing new sandwiches, they have a new value menu, um, as they're trying to capitalize on or or tap into people who are stretched right now because of gasoline prices or whatever else.

00:58 Speaker B

Um, they're introducing these new dirty drinks that they're talking about that are like sodas with other stuff in them. Um, and they also have what a new Red Bull drink that they're rolling out too. So they're, you know, they're throwing a lot out there to kind of like

01:14 Speaker A

Innovation.

01:15 Speaker B

Innovation. They're throwing a lot of innovations out there to see what's going to what's going to stick.

01:21 Speaker A

Menu innovation.

01:22 Speaker A

I think what's interesting uh for you know, and I some people might say that we shouldn't on this program be viewing it this way, but I think of us as looking at things through an investor lens versus a consumer lens.

01:37 Speaker A

From the investor's standpoint, the fast food story is moderately interesting, but not super interesting. Like this stock had some momentum, it hasn't been doing poorly, but it's kind of just been flattish, right? Over the last five years, stock's up 20%.

01:59 Speaker A

Um, things were looking, you know, when the US-Iran war broke out and oil prices surged, McDonald's, consumer staples, those were all in a bucket um that came into favor very quickly for investors. Stock's most recent high, you know, right around 340 bucks a share, uh right at the end of February, which is when the war broke out. And the stock had been on the rise ahead of that.

02:26 Speaker A

And I know that we see the executives on the call talking about um the macro environment looking more challenged. But the initial trade there was, well, if you've got higher gas prices and people have less wiggle in their household budget, they're going to come to our restaurants more often. Um but it just seems like that that has come out. That that theme has come out of the stock a little bit and I think this notion of there's a real durable trade down um with so much competition on on on the menu basis, on menu innovation.

03:04 Speaker A

doesn't seem to be super attractive to investors. Now that whole preamble is just because as a consumer, it's a really interesting time. There's like tons of new stuff on all these different places that you can now buy and the menus look completely different than they did five years ago. But for investors, it's kind of like, okay, thanks.

03:26 Speaker A

Stock's flat.

title: McDonald's misses US sales growth target as consumer spending tightens
content:
STORY: McDonald's missed its U.S. sales growth target in the first quarter.The world's biggest burger chain posted U.S. same‑store sales growth of 3.9% - below Wall Street estimates.Thursday's update showed low-price meal deals and limited-time offers struggled to draw diners.Consumers have recently pulled back on spending due to higher fuel and grocery costs.CEO Chris Kempczinski said the operating environment was still "challenging."That was depsite McDonald's beating quarterly estimates for revenue and profit.Several U.S. restaurant chains like Wingstop and Domino's have reported weaker quarterly sales growth.They cited a hit to customer spending from soaring gasoline prices caused by the Iran war.Wall Street analysts also argue lower-income consumers have turned more selective.It's seen buyers trade down to simpler, single‑item orders rather than full meals.Data from Placer.ai showed U.S. traffic was uneven at McDonald's through the first quarter.Same-store visits fell 1.3% in January due to winter storms.Traffic bounced back just under 4% in February on pent‑up demand, but slipped again in March.On a global scale, McDonald's found comparable sales rose 3.8% - slightly behind analyst forecasts.Although it was an improvement on last year's numbers.The firm's total revenue of $6.52 billion beat estimates.
